# Conditional age-length key example: European hake in the Adriatic Sea

European hake (*Merluccius merluccius*) in the Adriatic Sea (GFCM geographical subareas 17-18) was benchmarked in
2024 with a two-sex, multi-fleet Stock Synthesis model (FAO GFCM 2024). It is a good example for sex-structured
data: length compositions by sex for most fleets, conditional age-at-length data for the Italian trawl (ITA_OTB_18)
and longline (ITA_LLS_18) fleets in GSA 18, Richards growth by sex and a male natural mortality twice that of females.
This section goes through the diagnostics specific to such data and explains how to read them.

```{r hke-data, fig.height = 5}
hke <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hke.37.17-18", "hke.37.17-18.rds", package = "ss3diags2"))
ss3_fleets(hke)[, .(name, type, ncatch, nindex, nlen)]
lfh <- ss3_lencomp(hke)
lxh <- ss3_lencomp(hke, what = "exp")
ss3plot_data(catch = ss3_catch(hke), indices = ss3_indices(hke), lencomp = lfh)
```

## Growth by sex

`ss3_lhpar()` returns the growth parameters by sex (unit). The model uses Richards growth (Schnute
parameterisation); the curves of the plots use it, while `linf`, `k` and `t0` are a von Bertalanffy approximation
for FLicc:

```{r hke-growth, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 8}
lhh <- ss3_lhpar(hke)
lhh[c("L1", "L2", "A1", "A2", "K", "richards", "CVmin", "CVmax", "M"), ]
ss3plot_growth(hke, lfd = lfh)
```

> **Reading the growth plot.** Lines are the SS3 mean length at age by sex with $\pm$ 2 SD bands from the CV of
> length at age; horizontal lines are the largest observed length of each fleet. Females grow to about 80 cm at age
> 12, males to about 62 cm, and the sexes separate from about age 3. The bands set how far a fish of a given age can
> be from the mean: they are the key to the conditional age-at-length fits below. The Linf lines belong to the von
> Bertalanffy approximation (the Richards curve has no Linf of its own) and are only a guide.

## Length compositions and sex ratios

```{r hke-lenfit, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 10}
ss3plot_comps(lfh, fit = lxh, by = "unit", fleets = c("ITA_OTB_18", "ITA_LLS_18", "HRV_OTB_17", "MEDITS_ITA",
                                                      "MEDITS_HRV", "SOLEMON_17"))
```

With two sexes, the length compositions also carry the sex ratio. `ss3plot_sexratio()` shows the observed and
expected proportion of females by length (pooled over years) or by year (pooled over lengths). The bars are 95%
binomial (Wilson) intervals with the numbers in each bin, i.e. the adjusted sample sizes, so they show how far an
observed proportion can stray from the line by sampling alone. Bins with fewer than `min.n = 5` effective fish (mostly
the largest lengths) get no bar, since their interval would span most of 0-1; `ci = FALSE` removes the bars:

```{r hke-sexratio, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 10}
ss3plot_sexratio(lfh, fit = lxh)
ss3plot_sexratio(lfh, fit = lxh, type = "year")
```

> **Reading sex ratios.** Hake males grow more slowly and die faster (M 0.5 against 0.25), so the share of females
> rises with length to 100% above about 45 cm. The model follows this switch in all fleets, but in the Croatian
> trawl and surveys (HRV_OTB_17, MEDITS_HRV, and MEDITS_ITA above 25 cm) the observed switch is steeper: fewer
> females than expected at about 15-28 cm and more at about 30-40 cm. Males are more common among small fish and
> drop out of the intermediate lengths faster than modelled: male growth or male mortality differ from the model,
> selectivity differs between the sexes, or small hake are hard to sex. Where the bars of several neighbouring bins
miss the line on the same side (HRV_OTB_17 at 15-28 cm), the pattern is more than sampling noise. A sex ratio that drifts
> over years, away from the expected line, points to a time-varying process or a change in sampling.

## Conditional age-at-length

The conditional age-at-length compositions are strongly down-weighted (SS3 variance adjustments 0.01 and 0.11), so
with the adjusted sample size most length bins hold less than one fish and give no residual. With
`nsamp = "input"` the residuals use the number of aged fish per length bin:

```{r hke-caal, fig.height = 6.5, fig.width = 10}
cl <- ss3_resid(hke, quant = "con", long = TRUE, nsamp = "input")
ss3plot_caal(cl, fleet = "ITA_LLS_18", years = 2018:2023, lhpar = lhh)
ss3plot_caal(cl, fleet = "ITA_OTB_18", years = 2018:2023, lhpar = lhh)
```

> **Reading the conditional age-at-length plot.** Each panel is a year; x is age (females as circles to the left,
> males as triangles to the right of each age), y is length. Each row of bubbles (one length bin) is one sample: the
> ages of the fish of that length. The OSA residual compares the observed with the expected share of each age
> within the bin, conditioned from the youngest age up (blue: more fish of that age than expected; red: fewer).
> The curves are the SS3 growth by sex at the sampling time (solid females, dashed males) with $\pm$ 2 SD of length
> at age (grey).
>
> - **Diamonds and bars** are the observed and expected mean length at age of the aged fish. Both depend on how
>   the fish were selected by length (here longline fish are large for their age), so they are compared with each
>   other, not with the curve. A diamond away from its bar means the mean growth is off for that age and sex.
> - **Bubbles at the edges of the band** with one colour (blue above and red below the curve) mean length at age
>   varies more than the model's CV allows.
> - **A diagonal of one colour** moving one age per year is a year class with different growth.
>
> For Adriatic hake the observed means sit on the expected ones for both sexes and fleets, so the mean growth is
> consistent with the data: the males above the dashed curve on the longline are large-for-age fish caught by
> the gear, and the model expects them there. The residual pattern is in the spread: blue at the upper edges of
> ages 4-8 (longline) and ages 0-3 (trawl), red below. Length at age varies more than the fixed CVs (0.20 young,
> 0.10 old) allow, in particular for young fish: a sensitivity run estimating the CVs is the natural next step.
> The residuals use the input sample sizes, which the model down-weights, so their size (SD 1.5-2.4) shows
> overdispersion; the patterns, not the bubble sizes, matter.

The Francis weights of the conditional age-at-length data compare the mean age by length bin with its expected
value, combined over the bins of each year:

```{r hke-francis, fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 9}
fwc <- ss3_francis(hke, "con")
fwc
ss3plot_francis(fwc)
```

> **Reading the Francis weights.** The weight multiplies the current variance adjustment (`var_adj.new`). For
> ITA_OTB_18 it is `r round(fwc$w[1], 2)`, so the current adjustment of 0.01 is about right; for ITA_LLS_18
> `r round(fwc$w[2], 2)`, suggesting `r round(fwc$var_adj.new[2], 3)` instead of 0.11. The wide intervals
> (`r nrow(attr(fwc, "comps"))` years in total) show that these weights are only roughly determined.

## Runs tests and joint residuals

```{r hke-runs, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9}
ss3plot_runs(hke, quant = "con")
ss3_runs(hke, quant = "len")[, .(index, runs.p, test)]
ss3plot_jres(hke)
```

> **Reading the runs tests.** Both conditional age-at-length fleets fail the runs test of the mean age by length
> (p < 0.05): the mean ages at length run above or below the expected values for several years in a row. Together
> with the residual plots, this points to time-varying growth or variation in length at age that the model does not
> capture. The indices and the mean lengths of all fleets pass.
